name: Central banks vs energy inflation
backstory: The Iran war cut oil supply and pushed up headline inflation [the total price rise, including food and energy]. Central banks must decide whether that fades or leaks into wages and services, and after 2021 they are less willing to wait. The euro area hit 4% inflation, the Bank of England hiked to 4% last week, and the Fed sits at 3.875%.
today: The Fed minutes say officials expect more rate hikes and worry about AI's effect on inflation. The headlines do not give the full minutes text, so the details are unknown. Governor Barr said in a speech that inflation is too high and he expects it will be appropriate to raise rates further. Yesterday St. Louis Fed's Musalem said four more hikes may be needed. In the UK, inflation rose to 3.6% in October on record diesel prices. Bailey said it should reach about 5% by mid-next year, but he sees limited sign so far of knock-on effects on wages and other prices. He also said the rate path is not pre-set.

name: AI trade jitters
backstory: Markets have leaned on AI-linked mega-cap tech [the very largest companies by value], so doubts about AI spending hit the whole index. Nvidia's CEO left on Nov 12 and an AI selloff followed. The story has run since Nov 9.
today: The Nasdaq rose 0.42% while the S&P 500 and Dow fell, so AI was not a one-way selloff. Headlines say Nvidia's demand is 'hard to ignore' but four questions loom over the stock. Interim CEO Kress told staff 'let's move forward'. Palo Alto rose after earnings and a $4.5 billion deal for an AI startup. A Nov 19 headline says Anthropic's IPO raised over $81 billion, the largest offering on record, and one says it priced high. That was published after Tuesday's close, so it is not in today's closing data. The ECB warned that AI infrastructure is increasingly funded with debt, so a mood change could spread losses from stocks to bonds. A St. Louis Fed study says the ten hyperscalers spent nearly 13% of assets on capital spending [money for buildings and equipment] versus about 3% for other firms. A San Francisco Fed letter puts the CAPE ratio [a stock price divided by 10 years of average earnings, adjusted for inflation] at 40.5, below only the 43.1 peak of early 2000.

name: Iran war and oil
backstory: The conflict that began in early 2026 cut global oil output by 12 mb/d [million barrels per day] in March. Prices jumped but not to records, because the world was oversupplied and stored oil filled the gap. Tensions eased in June and then returned.
today: WTI fell 3.85% to 82.7 dollars as headlines pointed to supply-surplus expectations. Energy stocks slid, and Canada's TSX fell 2.1% on weak metals and energy. Yet the war still pushes energy costs up elsewhere. The ECB's Vujčić says it lifts European energy prices, the UK has record diesel prices, and Bailey says the conflict is in its ninth month.

name: US midterms and the dollar
backstory: The midterms produced what headlines call a Democratic rout. Markets ask how divided government would change tariffs, spending and the dollar. HSBC has said strong Democratic results could pressure the dollar near term.
today: The dollar index rose 0.31% to 103.81, and a headline calls it the biggest rally since 2024. Barclays and Deutsche Bank say the AI boom could extend dollar strength, and Jamie Dimon said the US will keep its reserve currency status. Today's move looks driven by Fed hike talk rather than the election, though no headline says so directly. The Canadian dollar fell to a 19-month low. Gold's 2.91% drop fits an earlier headline saying the dollar has flattened the 'debasement trade' [a bet that currencies lose value, so buy gold].

name: Yen defense
backstory: A weak yen pushed Japan to intervene [sell dollars to buy yen] in the currency market, including a record $50 billion in one day. The Bank of Japan's 1.25% rate is 2.625 percentage points below the Fed's 3.875%, which encourages selling yen to hold dollars.
today: USD/JPY fell 0.25% to 159.38, a small yen gain. Japan's economy unexpectedly shrank in Q3 as energy costs bit, and headlines say the dollar rally and Japan's slump leave the yen under pressure. A hawkish BOJ policymaker, Takata, called for a swift hike.
